title: Claude Code Hooks: Which Ones Add Tokens, Which Cut Them
content: The Claude Code hooks reference now lists 33 events, from SessionStart to ElicitationResult ( Anthropic hooks reference , read 2026-09-24). Most people meet hooks through a list of ten copy-paste examples: a linter after every edit, a desktop ping, a guard on rm -rf . Then they read that a hook cut someone's token usage by 42% or 90% and wonder whether their own hooks help or hurt. Both happen. A hook that prints to stdout on UserPromptSubmit adds its text to the conversation on every prompt you send. A hook that rewrites a tool call before it runs can stop a 3,000-line log from ever reaching the model. The difference sits in two details the example lists skip: which event the hook listens to, and which JSON field it returns. This article maps every token-relevant event to what it adds or removes, using only the official reference, and lists the traps that leave a hook silently doing nothing. TL;DR Four events add plain stdout to Claude's context: UserPromptSubmit , UserPromptExpansion
author: Paul Irolla
summary_zh: 文章梳理了 Claude Code hooks 参考文档中列出的 33 个事件，并逐一分析哪些 hook 会增加 token 消耗、哪些能减少 token 消耗。例如，在 UserPromptSubmit 事件里向 stdout 输出的内容，每次发送提示时都会加入对话上下文；而在 PreToolUse 阶段改写工具调用，可以避免数千行日志进入模型。文章指出，决定 hook 是增加还是减少 token 的关键有两点：监听的是哪个事件，以及返回的是哪个 JSON 字段。

title: Stop Claude Code from running dangerous commands with hooks
content: Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands, so why add anything? Because after the twentieth "Allow?" prompt in a session, most of us start clicking yes without reading, or we switch to a mode that stops asking. Instructions in CLAUDE.md like "never force-push to main" help, but they're text the model can forget or argue its way around. A hook is different. It's a program Claude Code runs before every tool call . If it says no, the command never runs, whatever the model was thinking. Claude gets the reason back and usually picks a safer approach. This post sets up three layers in about five minutes: A small PreToolUse hook for the catastrophic shell commands. Native permission deny rules for .env files. title: Your AI agent will lie to your customers. Here's how to catch it.
content: An AI support agent told a customer a $40 credit was applied. It wasn't, and then the agent told the operator to apply it. Skill Gate failed it in 5 of 5 runs, and it took 5 rounds of skill edits to get to 5 of 5 GREEN. What happened A customer wants a refund the policy doesn't cover, and they push. Your AI support agent drafts a confident reply: "I've applied that credit now; it will reduce what you owe." That's a $40 credit. No tool ran and nothing hit the billing system. title: I compared 12 AI coding agent memories. Most only remember what, not why
content: Your agent does not have a memory problem. It has a "why" problem. Every tool in this post can make an agent remember something tomorrow. A markdown file remembers what you typed into it. title: PHPStan First: The Gate Order I Use for AI-Written PHP Code
content: Originally published on my blog An AI agent writes PHP that looks right far more often than it is right. Turning on every quality tool at once doesn't fix that: the agent drowns in findings, and so do you. I add gates in a fixed order, sorted by how much each one catches per second it costs, and I set them up before I let the agent go fast. It's a useful signal: enterprise analytics agents are moving beyond returning SQL results toward multi-step calculations, statistical analysis, and scenarios. That introduces an important engineering question: what happens when step 1 returns plausible but semantically wrong data, and steps 2–5 faithfully build on it? title: I built Karpathy's LLM Wiki as a product — the hard part was stopping the LLM from writing
content: Every knowledge tool I tried failed in one of two directions. Notion, Obsidian, Roam: passive containers. They store beautifully and maintain nothing — you are the janitor, forever. NotebookLM and the RAG chatbots fail the other way: nothing accumulates. Ask a question and the answer is re-derived from raw chunks on the spot. Ask the same question next month and you pay the same derivation cost and get a slightly different answer. Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern flips this. Instead of retrieving at query time, the LLM maintains a persistent markdown wiki : it ingests your sources once, pre-bakes the cross-references, pre-flags the contradictions, and writes the synthesis down. Questions get answered from the wiki, not re-derived from the pile. title: Why We Treat the LLM as an Untrusted Planner
content: Giving AI access to your business software is easy. Making sure it uses that access responsibly is the real challenge. Imagine giving a new employee access to your company's database on their first day. They don't know your internal policies. They don't understand which customers are sensitive, which records should never be deleted, or which actions require a manager's approval. Would you give them unrestricted access to everything and simply tell them, "Please be careful"? Probably not. Yet, that's surprisingly close to how some people approach AI agents. They connect a large language model (LLM) to a database, an API, or a collection of internal tools. They write a detailed system prompt explaining what the AI should and shouldn't do. title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
content: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). title: The True Cost of LLM Hallucinations in Mobile Planning
content: Generative coding models accelerate syntax production, but unvetted outputs introduce silent architectural defects that evade compiler checks. The true cost of LLM hallucinations is paid in downstream debugging, where engineering teams spend valuable time untangling corrupted schemas and broken state. The durable answer is structured, human-verified specification before generating executable code. Key takeaways Syntax errors fail fast and carry minimal remediation overhead; silent semantic hallucinations pass CI checks and compound across the entire application lifecycle. Debugging a hallucinated schema after database migration consumes senior engineering time and depletes team runway. Multi-agent autonomous code generation compounds silent errors unless developers inspect intermediate schema and interface boundaries first. Pre-code specification of pillars, user stories, and data schemas intercepts hallucinated edge cases when intervention takes minimal effort. The hidden cost of LLM
author: HyunKi Lee
summary_zh: 文章指出，AI 编程模型产出代码虽快，但未经审查的输出会带来编译器发现不了的架构缺陷，例如 schema 损坏、状态错乱。这类语义层面的幻觉能通过 CI，修复代价远高于语法错误；多智能体自主生成代码时，问题还会层层累积。作者主张先由人写好并核对结构化规格，再让模型生成可执行代码。

title: An AI Agent Is Only as Safe as the Permissions Behind It
content: Giving an AI agent access to your business systems is easy to imagine. Knowing exactly what it can do when nobody is watching is the harder part. There's a question I think every business should ask before connecting an AI agent to its internal systems: If this agent makes a mistake, how much damage can it actually do? Not how smart is the model? Not how well does it follow instructions? And definitely not how impressive was the demo. How much damage can it do? Because there's a big difference between an AI agent that suggests which customer record needs updating and one that can actually update it. There's an even bigger difference between an agent that can read an order and one that can cancel every order in your database. Both might use the same language model. Both might sound equally confident. But their potential consequences are completely different. That difference comes down to permissions. title: Supplier Invoice Chatbot: 3-Provider Unified LLM API Automatic Fallback
content: A unified endpoint is the right boundary for an in-app chatbot that extracts supplier invoice fields, provided the application owns the quality checks and the router owns provider failover. Keep one provider-neutral request in the frontend, let the backend route across OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini, and record the chosen model, latency, and extraction result for every invoice. The useful before-and-after is small: Before: the UI knows provider names, each provider has a separate key, and a rate limit becomes a user-visible branch. After: the UI asks for an invoice extraction response, one API boundary selects a ready model, and the same request can move to another provider when the first is down or rate-limited. The trade-off is equally clear. A gateway can make switching cheap; it cannot make three different models produce identical field values. Treat failover as a continuity mechanism, then use a quality gate before writing invoice data to your system. This is the part to keep boring.

title: Apex Fusion Shows MIT's AI Agent Societies Do Not Need a Frontier Model to Work
content:
Apex Fusion Foundation reran MIT's SwarmWorld experiment with 50 agents on four consumer RTX 3090 GPUs in about 26 hours and 12,800 model calls, with MIT's code unchanged.
Nine of twelve paired effects matched MIT's direction, including every portfolio-resilience gain, which was larger in the replication.
A single Qwen3.8-27B agent reached 6 of 16 research milestones against 7 to 10 for MIT's model, while the society reached 16 of 16 against 14.
A hidden KV-cache precision setting changed results more than the gap between a 27B and a 235B model.

title: The Problem With Giving an AI Agent Too Much Freedom
content: An AI agent that can do everything might sound impressive. Until you realize that doing everything also means having more ways to get things wrong. There's something exciting about watching an AI agent work without constant supervision. You give it a task, it figures out the steps, calls a few tools, checks the results, and comes back with the job done. No endless back-and-forth. No clicking through a dozen screens. No waiting for someone to find the right button. It's easy to look at that experience and think: what if we just gave the agent more freedom? More tools. More access. Fewer restrictions. Let it figure things out. I understand the appeal. Honestly, the idea of software that can take a vague request and turn it into a completed task is one of the most interesting things happening in technology right now.
